boley-boley-1905-08.A1:
WESTERN NEGRO PRESS ASSOCIATION.
Marshal W. R. Shaver Killed. W. R. Shaver better known as Dick Shaver, was shot and killed by she outlaw, Dick Simmons, while Dick Simmons died from gun shot in the hands of Dick Shaver, two shots being fired by each. Mr. Shaver lives in Boley, and while he was serving as U.S. Deputy Marshall under Office Webb, he was also appointed as City Marshal for Boley, by the recently elected officers of Boley. Mr. Shaver is both widely and favorably known throughout the Territory. The killing occurred about 8 of clock. Dick Shaver went out three miles to Simpson's house to arrest him for horse stealing. While Shaver was standing about twenty feet from the fence of George Johnson talking, Simmons came from a blind road around the fence at Shaver's book, and without warning fired on Shaver with a winchester. As Shaver saw Simmons she dismounted his horse and fired on Simmons. Each man fired two shots. From the facts given by the coroner, one of of Simmon's shots missed Shaver; but Shaver is a noted markman, and both of his shots hit his mark (Simmons), either of which would have been fatal. The shot that sent Mr. Shaver to his untimely death pierced the stomach coming out at the back, three inches to the right of the backbone. While Simmons had his gun to his shoulder taking aim, Shaver fired on him, the ball going through the left hand riddling it, passing on through arm into the breast, just above the heart servering the arteries. The two shots were within about an inch of the other, either of which would caused instant death. The coroner's jury cendered a verdict according to the facts above given. Shaver lived about half an hour after being shot. His remains were brought back to Boley, ex interment. Mr. Shaver has lived in the Territory since boyhood and knew every corer and corer. Mr. Shaver leaves a wife and four small brothers to mourn his loss, besides four brothers, one of which happened to be in Boley from Eufaula, I. T. about the time of the tragedy. Mr. Shaver was buried Tuesday under the auspices of Enterprise Lodge No. 6132 G. U. O. O. F. Pursuant to the regular appointment under the Provisions of the Cousintitution, the Western Negro Press Association of the United States of America is hereby called to convene at Muskogee, I. T., in its Ninth Annual Session, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday September 20th, 21st and 22nd, 1905. All proprietors, editors, managers and correspondents west of Mississippi River are eligible to membership in said association and are urged to be present. We cordially extend an invitation to the members of the fraternity and the friends of the newspapers in general throughout the country, to meet with us at Muskogee to consider those questions so vital to the welfare of the race in the United States of America. We also extend and expect all ministers and college professors business men and professional men and women to join in this coming meeting. Recent development shows the need of action on the part of the intelligent and thoughtful members of the race, and the Press with the aid of the Pulpit must undoubtedly take the lead. The official program that will be published later will be up to the usual high standard. We would again urge upon every paper and its entire staff to make this meeting a personal matter in order to secure a large and enthusiastic gathering.
boley-boley-1905-08.A3:
KILL EACH OTHER.
United States Deputy Marshal and Man He Wanted Dead.
Guthrie, Aug. 18.—Ed Shaffer, a deputy United States marshal, was sent into Lincoln county to arrest Dick Simmons, charged with horse stealing. Near Boley, a negro settlement, Simmons stepped from behind a clump of bushes and shot Shaffer down. Raising on an elbow Shaffer shot and killed Simmons and five minutes later was also a corpse.
boley-boley-1905-08.A5:
TWO TOWNS IN TERROR
Negro Populace Fear Attack From Criminal Gang Seeking Revenge.
It is authoritatively reported that Andy Simmons, the most desperate of the entire Simmons gang of outlaws, and on whose head there now is a price for the murder of a deputy marshal, has returned to his home near Boley and sent word to the colored officials and inhabitants of the little town, that they should prepare to die, as he is deeply incensed over the killing of his brother and the arrest of the two younger brothers and that he is organizing a posse of bad men that will swoop down upon the town and kill off the negroes.

The population has been in a state of frenzy since the double tragedy of last Wednesday, and Saturday night it was deemed necessary to have an extra force of police and marshals detailed to guard the outskirts of the town, to prevent a surprise attack on the town by the outlaws at night. Andy Simmons is perhaps six feet or more in height, presenting a formidable physical appearance, is known to be cruel and reveneful and possessed of a daring and cool headed fearlessness seldom encountered even among the most desperate criminals. It is said that at the funeral of the brother who was shot and killed by the town marshal, Schaffer, the mother of the nine boys wept bitterly over the grave of her dead son and said: "This is not the end of the trouble; there will be more deaths; Andy will have revenge."

At Paden the inhabitants are terrified and the officials there who assisted with the capture and arrest of Lewis, the younger brother, are armed and prepared to resist an attack at any time by the gang. Many of the negroes who live in the two towns and on farms adjoining the ranch of the Simmons family are leaving their homes and going to other towns farther removed from the scene of the disturbance. Superstition and ignorance, together with incredible rumors started by irresponsible persons, are largely responsible for the condition of confusion and inability of the officers to properly organize the populace so that an attack on the part of the outlaws could be successfully resisted.

charles-julius-miller-pittsburg-1905-08-.A1:
PITTSBURG RACE RIOT.
Fight Because Waiter Would Not Serve Negro in Restaurant.
(By Telegraph to The Tribune.)
Aug. 22—Two hundred pe

Pittsburg, Aug. 22.—Two hundred people engaged in a desperate race riot late this evening at Luna Park, and as a result a number of persons were injured. Charles Julius Miller, a negro, employed in the Registry Department of the Chicago Postoffice, entered the Café Neapolitan. Miller is here attending the National Convention of the colored Knights of Pythias. Waiters refused to serve him, and Miller, when ordered out by the waiter, abused him. One of the waiters attempted to strike Miller with a chair, and he drew a revolver. A number of shots were fired before the weapon could be taken from him. Friends ran to his assistance and a free-for-all fight followed. Fifteen persons were arrested. Miller, who was seriously injured, and several others had to be sent to hospitals.

Two Hundred People Engage in Battle at Suburb of Pittsburg.

Charles Julius Miller, a Negro employed in the registry department of the Chicago post office, entered the Cafe Neapolitan with a Negro woman. Miller is here attending the national convention of the Colored Knights of Pythias.

Waiters refused to serve him and Miller, when ordered out, became abusive. One of the waiters attempted to strike him with a chair, when Miller drew a revolver. A large number of shots were fired before the weapon could be taken from him. Friends of Miller ran to his assistance and a free-for-all fight started. A riot call was sent in, and about fifty persons were arrested. Miller, who was seriously injured, and several others, had to be sent to hospitals. I Told You So—Palladium.

A young woman once sat at a boarding-house table beside a reserved and awkward country boy whom she delighted to tease. When she left she asked him to write in her autograph album. The poem which John G. Whittier wrote there, and which has just been published for the first time, stands as a warning to other young ladies that she who laughs first at a seemingly dumb countryman may be herself laughed at many years later. Banana Supply Short.

CHICAGO, AUG. 15.—With the supply of bananas reduced to less than half the usual amount because of the uarantine at New Orleans, dealers here are predicting a famine in this fruit. Prices are about double those of a month ago.

Naval Critic Dead.

LONDON, AUG. 15.—Sir William Laird Clowes died to-day. He was born in 1856 and was known best as a naval critic, historical and miscellaneous writer.

CORDELE, GA., AUG. 15.—Two negroes were killed outright and three fatally injured to-day near Oakfield by a woodsman named Malfis, whom they had waylaid. The negroes had clubs and knives and Malfis a revolver.

PHILADELPHIA, AUG. 15.—Logan Hall, in which is the anatomical and surgical department of the Pennsylvania University Medical School, was damaged by fire last night to the extent of $40,000. The greatest loss was entailed by the breaking of microscopes and other delicate instruments.

KNOXVILLE, TENN., AUG. 15.—Damage suits aggregating $40,000 were filed in the Federal Court at Greenville to-day by four Mormon missionaries, who charge they were roughly handled in Greene County, when they attempted to preach Mormon doctrines.

J. H. Davis Will Use It as a Country Seat.

Boscobel Island, in the Hudson, between Crugers and Oscawanna, has been purchased by J. H. Davis, a rich New Yorker, who intends to lay out a fine country seat. This island is one of the most picturesque along the eastern shore of the Hudson River. henry-sterling-baconton-1905-08-17.A2:
Negro Charged With Peonage.
Macon, Ga., August 17.—William Strickland, a negro farmer arrested by federal officers near Valdosta, is held in Macon under a charge of peonage. This is the first time the net of this law has been thrown for a negro citizen in the history of the federal courts here and since the act was instituted for the benefit of the blacks this case promises to prove a novel one. Strickland is accused of holding a negro boy in servitude and beating him when he ran away from his employer with a small amount of money. Strickland will have a trial before Commissioner Martin shortly.
henry-sterling-baconton-1905-08-17.A7:
ACCUSED OF PEONAGE.
The Charge is Brought Against a Negro for Holding a Black Boy.
(By the Associated Press.)
aldosta Ga Aug 22 —Depu

(By the Associated Press.)
Valdosta, Ga., Aug. 22.—Deputy United States Marshal Godwin has returned from Baconton, where he arrested a negro, William Strickland, on the charge of violating the peonage law. It is claimed that Strickland has been holding a negro boy named Henry Sterling, in "involuntary servitude." Strickland got the boy in South Carolina and kept him at work. He whipped the boy and the boy ran away, whereupon Strickland is said to have had him arrested under the labor contract law. He then had the boy released on his promise to work out the matter, and has since held the boy in his service, according to the report. The boy complained to some other negroes and they took the matter up against Strickland.
Stricklands bond was fixed at $300 and the boy was placed in jail to await the hearing, being held as a witness at $1 a day.

samuel-edwards-st-louis-1905-08-16.A1:
TWO SHOT WHILE ON STREET CAR Shots Fired at Negro, on Broadway and Olive, Strike Passengers in Legs. ONE MAN IS ARRESTED. Another, Believed to Be a Party to Wounding, Escapes—Injuries to Those Hit Prove Slight.
Following an attack upon Clarence Hunt, a negro boy, on an Olive street car at 1:30 this morning, as the car neared Broadway, two passengers, who had no part in the controversy, were shot and one of the assailants of Hunt was arrested.

The wounded men gave their names as John Rogers of No. 236 Old Manchester road and Sam Edwards of No. 288 North Jefferson avenue. Edwards is a negro.

Another man, who was said to have been with the man who fired the shots, managed to make his escape.

The car was crowded at the time, and when the shooting began there was a wild scramble on the part of everyone to get under seats and through the front door.

The negro boy, Clarence Hunt, over whom the row started, was sleeping on a seat at the back end of the car.

At Broadway a gang of young fellows boarded the car, and one of them noticed Hunt sleeping. He grasped him by the legs and pulled him into the aisle. The boy, wishing to avoid trouble, went to the farther end of the car and took a seat.

Several passengers interfered to prevent trouble, and the men got off. As they did so one of them remarked, "He's only a nigger, anyhow." Then came the flash of a revolver, and one man began firing through the car at the negro boy. One man, endeavoring to get out of harm's way, was hit in the thigh, while another, farther up the car, was hit in the ankle.

The shooting attracted a crowd of persons who were waiting for cars, and the police, hearing the noise, ran toward the cars. The men ran north on Broadway, but one was arrested.

He is known as Thomas Lamb. He was taken to the Chestnut Street Station-house by Sergeant Flannigan and Patrolmen Farrell and O'Brien, who made the arrest. Clarence Hunt was also taken to the station-house as a witness.

The two injured men were removed to the City Dispensary in the ambulance.

The wounds in their legs were found to be more painful than serious. According to statements made by Lamb when taken to the Chestnut Street Station, the police believe that he did not do the shooting himself. They imagine, however, that he may be shielding some man who did. Lamb gave his address as No. 300 Pine street. He said he was a former police officer. He is held pending investigation.

sack to Be Executed Together at 6 O'Clock Monday Morning.

Chief Deputy Sheriff Edward Eisleben and Deputy Sheriff Joe Kelley yesterday tested the gallows in the jail yard upon which Lambert Niehaus and Henry J. Heusack, convicted murderers, are to be hanged Monday at 6 a. m. The men will be hanged at the same time. The deputies oiled the hinges of the trap and found them to be in perfect working order.

The finishing touches were put on the gallows by the workmen yesterday, as some repairs had to be made. The gallows was thoroughly cleaned and a new railing built.

Niehaus shot and killed Thomas Fluegel, his brother-in-law, December 20, 1993. He is 4 years old.

Heusack killed August Raphael, his father-in-law, March 16, 1963, with a hatchet, crushing the skull of his relative. Heusack is 55 years old.

A death watch will be placed over the condemned men Saturday.

When the Kentuckian got so he could see, he started to violate the fifteenth amendment. It took four men to pry him off.

"If you had asked me for it as though I was a human being and not a mere incumbrance, sir, you would have received it," said the negro in Harvard English.

"Well, by the gods, this is sure Yankee land," said the Kentuckian. He was led away searching his soul for language to express his feeling.

This same Kentuckian sat in the palm garden last night and entertained a full table. The waiter was bustling about behind him. All of a sudden the Kentuckian's golf cap was knocked off. He could feel some one reaching around under his chair looking for it. The Kentuckian was at a violent point in the story; he kept right on. He felt a tap on his shoulder; he simply reached up his hand, took the cap and went on talking without so much as looking back.

He supposed it was the waiter, but it wasn't. It was Mr. Sato. When Mr. Sato turned at the door and looked back with a smile that was half pain the Kentuckian saw the point and wilted. All the morning he was hunting Mr. Sato with an apology.

Mr. Korostovitz has a toothache. He has been going about for three or four days with a fine swelling under his blond beard.
A Portsmouth dentist told him to wait a day or two and the swelling would go down.
At midnight last night the pain got past all bearing. He called for an auto, but the regular autos were gone to bed. At that moment along came Gov. McLane's chauffeur, with the Governor's car. He volunteered and carried the Russian Secretary to Portsmouth, where the tooth was pulled.

POKOTILOFF BEATS THE LAUNDRY.

M. Pokotiloff, the giant Minister to Pekin, has met the American laundry and it is his'n. We have a most charmingly irresponsible laundry up here. When you send out any clothes you make out two lists, one for the hotel and one for yourself. You add your name, date of birth, mother's maiden name, color of your eyes and hair, state of weather and general remarks. The negro bellhoy carries it away. A few weeks later, strolling in the basement, you see a familiar bosom; it is your shirt, all your shirts, still there.

WITTE WATCHES THE DANCERS.

It has been rather a field night here, recalling the first few nights of the conference, when the show was new. There is a dance on in the ballroom. Witte and Rosen honored it with their presence. They did not dance, but they stood in the doorway and watched Takeshita, Hanahira and Sato of the opposition whirling American girls, whose heads just topped their shoulders to the tune of the Tenth Artillery band.

While Mr. Witte watched the dancing the band played a tune he liked. He applauded and asked: "What tune was that?"

"Peggy O'Grady," some one answered.

"I wish they would play it again," said Witte. The Russian secretary translated this to the bandmaster, who ordered two encores for Mr. Witte's benefit.

ON THE FUNNY BONE ON THE FUNNY BONE. Army Life. Since reading in the press about This sad domestic strife An army man, I've doped it out, Must lead a lovely life. When'er an army man wakes up, Aroused by breakfast gong. His servant fetches him a cup Containing liquors strong. He has a dip and dons his clothes, Nor lingers long to drink. But to the buffet straightway goes, And takes a real drink. The time 'till dinner he puts in With comrades glad and gay. Consuming whisky, rum and gin In an informal way. But after dinner strict are things, And all must be just so; To juleps and the like he clings, For none but mixed drinks go. But when the routine of the day At eventide is o'er Into his hide in his own way The liquor he may pour. Oh, soldiers live upon a stern And coldly rigid plan. But still I very often yearn To be an army man. Left In the Lurch.

PAYS A QUARTER FOR
BIG COLORADO FARM.

[Paducah News-Democrat.]

For twenty-five cents Miss Lula Reed, of this city, drew a farm in Colorado, 160 acres in extent. Miss Reed has just been notified of her luck, and is only awaiting the return of her father, Judge W. M. Reed, from Michigan, to comply with the requirements and take possession.

It was while Miss Reed was making a trip through the West recently with Miss Jean Todd, of Owensboro, that she invested her quarter so profitably. In passing through Grand Junction, Col., she was asked to take a chance on 8,000 acres of land, which had been split up into quarter sections by a large land-owning company, to be given away. There were 30,000 other chances, but Miss Reed decided she would take one any way.

Yesterday came the news that she was one of the lucky ones.

Alexander's Magazine For July.
Under the heading of "The Negro's Passing Opportunity," the above is clipped from The New York Tribune. What it asserts is partly true and can be fully accepted by our people in the same spirit in which it is written. But The Tribune does not understand fully the conditions of affairs in many sections of the south. One of the main reasons why so many of our people leave the farms and rural districts is because of ill treatment accorded them by a certain class of white planters, from which they have no redress whatever. Should any of them at any time resent the most heinous wrong heaped upon them, they generally get the worst of it as was demonstrated in a nearby county some weeks ago. Because a colored man refused to work faster when the thermometer was near the century mark, he was cursed and otherwise abused, he and a son was shot down and another one had to run for his life. The white man who committed the act was not molested. This is one reason for the scarcity of farm helps in this section. Many more instances can be sighted. While what is sighted above is a fact yet there are many white farmers in this state who are humane in their treatment and who do everything possible to encourage their helpers. Notwithstanding the disadvantages under which they labor there are hundreds of prosperous colored farmers, in the state, and their thriftiness should be emulated by others.
